sections.h2: Is selling in Freehold Township, NJ the same as selling in Freehold Borough?
sections.html:
No. Freehold Township and Freehold Borough are separate municipalities with separate offices, and the township completely surrounds the borough. New Jersey counts this as one of 21 pairs of doughnut towns, where one municipality wraps around another, so check which one your deed and tax bill name before you call anyone.

The township covers 38.65 square miles of land in western Monmouth County. The Census Bureau estimates 36,052 residents for July 2025, up 1.9% from the April 2020 base but still below the 36,184 counted in 2010.

Homes here skew toward owners: 83.7% of housing is owner-occupied, and 94.2% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Median value of owner-occupied homes is $553,600 for 2020-2024, with median gross rent of $2,194.

sections.h2: How does Freehold Township's history show up in a house sale today?
sections.html:
It shows up in the street names, the farmland and the parks. The township was first formed on October 31, 1693, and the legislature incorporated it on February 21, 1798. The word freehold is an English legal term for fee simple ownership, which is the kind of title you are transferring.

The Battle of Monmouth was fought on June 28, 1778, on ground now preserved as Monmouth Battlefield State Park, partly inside the township. Later, highways such as U.S. Route 9 and Route 33 let residents commute to Newark, Philadelphia and New York, and large neighborhoods of single-family homes followed.

Commercial growth came in layers. Brockway Glass built a plant off Center Street in 1955 and closed it in 1991, 3M opened a tape plant in 1957, CentraState Medical Center opened in 1971 as Freehold Area Hospital, and Freehold Raceway Mall opened in 1990 as the second largest mall in the state. Farms with crops, thoroughbreds, sod and orchards still operate in the township.

sections.h2: What does Freehold Township require before a house can be sold?
sections.html:
Freehold Township requires both a Certificate of Continued Occupancy (CCO) inspection and a fire inspection whenever a residential property is sold or rented. The two applications must go to the Housing Department together, each with its own check or money order, and the township does not take cash or cards.

The inspection appointment can be scheduled only after both applications and payments are in. A CCO issued for a resale is valid for up to 120 calendar days, or until occupancy changes, so do not apply so early that it lapses before closing. For scheduling, call the Department of Zoning and Housing Enforcement at 732-294-2066.

sections.h2: What does the Freehold Township inspector look for?
sections.html:
The township's own checklist is mainly about safety and open permits, and it states that buyers should still hire a private inspector. Any violation the inspector considers a safety issue must be fixed even if it is not on the list.

  • Permits: work done without permits, such as water heaters, furnaces, AC, decks, sheds, fences and finished basements, must be permitted and closed first.
  • Utilities must be on, and the house number must be six inches high and visible from the street.
  • Doors: entry doors with deadbolts need an inside thumb latch, and double-key deadbolts and slide bolts are not allowed.
  • Electrical: GFCI outlets within six feet of every sink, and covers on all outlets, switches and junction boxes.
  • Garage: entry doors need a solid core wood or steel door with a 20-minute fire rating.
  • Dryer vents must be flexible metal, and a sump pump needs its own outlet and must discharge outdoors.
  • Pools need self-closing, self-latching gates and must be running or closed.

Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are handled on the separate fire checklist. Alarms are required on every level including the basement and within ten feet of bedrooms, and detectors must be replaced every ten years.

sections.h2: What if the Freehold Township house cannot pass the CCO before closing?
sections.html:
The township offers a document called Transfer of Title, No Occupancy, which lets a closing go forward while the buyer fixes the remaining items. The state still requires every property to pass the fire inspection before the sale, so the smoke and carbon monoxide work cannot be skipped.

The process runs in steps. Both applications and payments go in first, and the inspector lists deficiencies, sometimes marking the house as having too many items to list. The buyer's attorney then writes a letter on the township's sample, agreeing there will be no occupancy until a new inspection and CCO, and agreeing to hold the township harmless. After the fire inspection passes and the letter is filed, the Housing Department emails the document for closing.

After closing the buyer owns the repair list and schedules the final CCO inspection. This path suits a cash buyer who plans to renovate. Rental properties follow stricter rules: they must be registered, vacant at inspection, freshly painted and, if built before 1978, supported by a lead-safe certificate that lasts two years.

sections.h2: How do estates, trusts and co-owners handle state forms at a Freehold Township closing?
sections.html:
Each seller on the deed completes a GIT/REP residency form, and the Monmouth County Clerk will not record the deed without one. Married couples who file a joint New Jersey return can sign one form, but unmarried co-owners each sign their own.

  • Estates: the estate completes the form under its own residency status, signed by the executors or the administrator if there was no will. One form can carry several executors' signatures.
  • Trusts: the trustee signs for the trust, and a trustee who is also a beneficiary signs a second form in a personal capacity.
  • Percent of ownership: if one owner holds 50% and two others hold 25% each, each form shows that share.
  • LLCs and corporations complete the GIT/REP-3 and check the box for sellers that are not individuals.

For a nonresident seller, the state's formula multiplies gain by 10.75% but never lets the estimated payment fall below 2% of the deed consideration. Sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales are the only exceptions to the form requirement.

sections.h2: What do roads, schools and employers mean for Freehold Township buyers?
sections.html:
Buyers weigh the commute first. Mean travel time to work is 30.9 minutes (2020-2024). Route 9, Route 33, Route 18 and Route 79 cross the township, with county routes 522, 524, 527 and 537, and Interstate 195 is reachable through Howell on Route 9 or Jackson on County Route 537. Garden State Parkway Exit 100 is about ten miles east.

NJ Transit buses 131, 135 and 139 run along Route 9 to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. The nearest rail stops are Aberdeen-Matawan, Asbury Park and Long Branch, and the SeaStreak ferry from Highlands is a 25 to 30 minute drive from the east side of the township.

High school students attend Freehold Township High School or Freehold High School, both in the Freehold Regional High School District, and assignment depends on the home address. CentraState Medical Center, a 287-bed hospital inside the township, ranks as the county's fourth-largest employer. The township sits on the northern edge of the humid subtropical climate zone, next to the humid continental zone.

faqs.q: Does Freehold Township require an inspection when I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. Freehold Township requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy inspection and a fire inspection for every residential sale or rental. Both applications are submitted together to the Housing Department, each with a check or money order.

faqs.q: How long is a Freehold Township resale CCO good for?
faqs.a: Up to 120 calendar days from the date of issue, or until the occupancy changes, whichever comes first. A rental CCO lasts only up to 60 days.

faqs.q: Can a Freehold Township house close without passing the CCO?
faqs.a: Yes, with a Transfer of Title, No Occupancy document. The buyer's attorney signs a letter agreeing there is no occupancy until the final CCO is issued, and the property must still pass the fire inspection first.

faqs.q: Which phone number do I call to schedule a Freehold Township CCO?
faqs.a: Call the Department of Zoning and Housing Enforcement at 732-294-2066. The township's FAQ also lists 732-294-5109, and the zoning office line is 732-294-2068.

faqs.q: Do estates in Freehold Township need special state tax forms?
faqs.a: They need the same GIT/REP form as any seller, filled out in the estate's name. If there was a will, the executors or beneficiaries who sign the deed sign the form; with no will, the administrator signs it.
